title: Accelerated Parallel Tempering via Neural Transports
one_liner: Speed up parallel tempering by letting learned proposal maps move samples between nearby temperature levels with less mismatch.
lead: Parallel tempering is a sampling method for hard probability shapes with many separated high-probability regions. It runs many chains at different temperatures and swaps their states so hot chains can explore widely while cold chains stay close to the target. The trouble is that adjacent temperature levels may still look too different, so swap attempts fail often. This paper inserts learned transport maps between those levels. The maps push samples toward shapes that overlap more, so swap information can travel across the ladder with less waste while the method keeps the long-run guarantees of classical parallel tempering.

problem.h2: Why plain parallel tempering stalls on hard sampling problems
paras: Suppose you need draws from a probability shape with several distant peaks. One Markov chain can get trapped in one peak for a long time. Parallel tempering tries to fix that by running many copies of the chain. The hottest copy sees a flatter version of the target, so it can move across peaks more easily. Lower-temperature copies stay closer to the exact target.

The whole scheme depends on swaps between neighboring temperatures. If the two neighboring shapes barely overlap, a state that looks reasonable at one level looks implausible at the next level. Then swap attempts fail, so discoveries made by hot chains do not reach the cold chain that matters most. The usual repair is to add many more temperature levels, but that raises compute cost because every extra level needs its own chain.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Learn transport maps between neighboring temperature levels so states line up better, because better overlap makes swaps useful instead of mostly rejected.

paras: Classical parallel tempering changes temperature only through swaps between raw states. This paper adds learned transport maps between neighboring temperatures so the swap proposal itself is adapted to the gap between those two levels.
object.object: the state passed between neighboring temperature levels

hidden.name: neighbor overlap
paras: The quantity that decides whether parallel tempering works is overlap between neighboring tempered targets. Overlap means that a state judged plausible at one level is still plausible at the next level. If overlap is tiny, swaps almost never pass.

The learned map targets this quantity directly. It does not try to solve the whole sampling problem in one shot. Instead it makes local bridges less awkward, because each bridge only needs to translate between two nearby levels rather than from the easiest level all the way to the final target.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the local overlap terms that decide whether swaps carry useful information.

reads.html: The main question is whether one temperature level can hand a state to the next level without that state looking out of place.
The transport maps raise swap utility because they increase effective overlap between adjacent tempered targets.

paras: Parallel tempering already has a good global structure: hot levels discover distant regions, and cold levels refine exact samples. Its weakness is local communication between levels. The paper repairs that local communication by training a learned proposal that says, in effect, 'if this state came from level k, where should a comparable state sit at level k plus one?'

That repair helps because swap acceptance depends on local agreement. A transport that preserves high-probability regions maps states into places where the neighboring level assigns similar weight. Then the acceptance test rejects fewer good moves. Fewer rejected moves matter because information about distant peaks can travel down the ladder instead of dying at one badly matched boundary.

The method still keeps the standard acceptance correction, so the learned map does not need to be exact. It only needs to make proposals land in better places often enough that the corrected chain moves through the state space more freely, because accepted cross-level moves let discoveries from hot chains reach the cold chain.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the cold chain sits near peak A and the warmer neighbor has found peak B.
Without transport, the raw warmer state looks implausible to the cold chain, so the swap ratio comes out near 0.1 and the swap is usually rejected.
With transport, the warmer state is moved toward a cold-level point that still represents peak B but better matches the cold density.
Now the ratio can rise to about 0.7, so the swap often passes.
That accepted swap matters because the cold chain can now continue exploring peak B instead of staying trapped near peak A.

math.note: The acceptance correction keeps the target exact in the long run, while the learned map changes only how often useful proposals are offered.

charts.title: Classical parallel tempering
charts.note: Many levels are needed because neighboring targets still mismatch, so the method spends work maintaining chains that mainly protect swap acceptance.

charts.title: Transport-assisted parallel tempering
charts.note: The learned bridge reduces local mismatch, so fewer levels can still pass information through the ladder.

items.b: Transport fit can miss rare regions.
items.html: If the learned map is trained on samples that never visit one important peak, it cannot learn how to move states into that region. Then the method still misses that peak because the proposal bridge never points there.

items.b: Neighbor levels can still be too far apart.
items.html: A learned map cannot rescue an absurdly sparse ladder. If two temperatures describe very different shapes, the corrected proposal may still land in low-probability zones and swaps will still fail.

items.b: Training cost can outweigh the gain on easy targets.
items.html: If the target has one broad peak, plain parallel tempering may already move well enough. Then learning transports adds extra work without much return because overlap was not the bottleneck.
The method pays off on multimodal targets because local bridges matter most when raw swaps would otherwise block travel between distant peaks.

paras: Build a two-dimensional target with three separated peaks and compare three samplers: one ordinary chain, classical parallel tempering, and transport-assisted parallel tempering. Track how often the cold chain visits all peaks, how many swap attempts are accepted, and how many steps are needed before the cold chain's histogram matches the true target. The paper's point is visible if the transport-assisted version reaches all peaks with fewer temperature levels because the local bridges let discoveries move across the ladder.
demo.metric_eq: coverage_gap = sum over peaks of |estimated_peak_mass - true_peak_mass|
demo.closing: The demo should show that the learned bridges matter at the level of accepted swaps, and that those accepted swaps matter because they improve the final cold-chain coverage of all peaks.
